OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on
Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination

Jie Huang Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology Email: mailto:jhuang@ir.hit.edu.cnjhuang@ir.hit.edu.cn    Yuecheng Hong Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology Email: mailto:2023112391@stu.hit.edu.cn2023112391@stu.hit.edu.cn    Yao Chen Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Shengding Jiao Affiliation: Peking University    Xudong Liu Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology    Qiang Ye Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
Abstract

In many long-horizon settings, an agent’s own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

1 Introduction

Long-running agents often make choices that change both the resources available for future work and the obligations they will need to meet (Brehmer, 1992; Kumar et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026). The value of these choices depends on how later decisions maintain or revise the resource arrangements they create (Sun et al., 2023; You et al., 2026). Consider a rental manager with one tent available today. Renting it earns immediate income but may leave it unavailable for a more valuable trip later. Holding it preserves that opportunity, whose arrival and value remain uncertain. Once the manager accepts a future booking, an intervening rental also affects an existing obligation: serving both customers requires enough time for the tent to return, be cleaned, and become ready again. Later rental decisions must therefore weigh new opportunities against the capacity needed for commitments already made (Zhang and Cheung, 2022).

Recent business benchmarks evaluate agents through continuing operations, including purchasing, pricing, and customer management (Andon Labs, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), as well as contract selection and financing decisions with lasting consequences (He et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026). Less attention has been given to how agents jointly maintain the feasibility of their own commitments and reassess resource allocations as opportunities change.

To address this gap, we introduce OutfitterBench, a benchmark in which agents manage a simulated outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days. Its design draws on work linking planning with the evaluation of alternatives (Bratman et al., 1988) and examining how existing plans change the value of new options (Horty and Pollack, 2001). We focus on two coupled demands. Intertemporal feasibility maintenance requires keeping changing asset states, accepted work, and subsequent actions compatible. Intertemporal resource valuation and reallocation requires comparing competing uses of equipment-time and capital when forming commitments and revisiting existing allocations.

In OutfitterBench, advance reservations and uncertain walk-in demand draw from a shared fleet whose availability changes through rental, return, cleaning, and maintenance. New rentals can undermine the supply supporting earlier bookings; protecting those bookings can exclude more valuable uses. The agent chooses bookings and prices, arranges supply, and limits walk-in use. It can negotiate changes or cancel a booking at a compensation cost. Purchases and sales reshape future supply; once the fixed equipment-capital ceiling binds, new investment may require replacing existing assets. The environment combines a product catalog derived from Taobao listings and historical Beijing weather with models of customer demand and equipment operations. The objective is to maximize terminal value: cash plus eligible equipment resale value minus outstanding liabilities.

We compare 7 model configurations with a public-information rule policy on the same 2 world seeds. Figure 1 summarizes the resulting value paths. The rule policy outperforms several agents, while only the leading agent exceeds it in both worlds. Agents can serve more bookings and still lose business value. Some agents repeatedly schedule equipment without allowing for turnaround; stronger runs sometimes overlook other affected commitments when preparing supply across days. Reliable fulfillment can also coexist with lower rents for comparable bookings, investment assessments that fail to guide later asset choices, and protection limits that exclude usable rental intervals. The leading agent more often connects supply preparation with these economic comparisons, although local counterfactual tests reveal remaining opportunities for more profitable equipment use. Taken together, these findings reveal limits in agents’ ability to keep successive decisions compatible and to reassess resource allocations as the value of competing uses changes.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    A benchmark for long-horizon resource allocation and commitment coordination. We introduce OutfitterBench, a continuing rental environment that couples dynamic asset availability, agent-chosen future obligations, and uncertain opportunities under a long-term business-value objective.

  2. 2.

    A comparative evaluation of LLM agents. We evaluate agents against a public-information rule-based baseline on matched world seeds, revealing substantial differences in long-term business value, with several agents underperforming the baseline.

  3. 3.

    A systematic analysis of intertemporal decisions. We combine trajectory analysis with state-based diagnostics, matched-booking comparisons, and local counterfactual tests. The analysis identifies failures to carry constraints across decisions, weaker returns from comparable commitments, and gaps between investment assessments and subsequent resource choices.

The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

2 Related Work

Interactive and Long-Horizon Agent Benchmarks.

Interactive benchmarks evaluate tool use, policy adherence, and actions with observable consequences (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024). Workplace and cross-session workflows extend these demands to coordinating tools and using information from earlier interactions (Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), while games and discovery environments examine sustained exploration, strategic decisions, and adaptation to evolving states or unfamiliar rules (Paglieri et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025).

Continuing business simulations connect repeated operating decisions to long-term outcomes. Vending-Bench 2, FoodTruck Bench, RetailBench, and related e-commerce environments couple sourcing, pricing, inventory, and cash flow (Andon Labs, 2025; FoodTruck Bench, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Project and enterprise simulations examine contract selection, investment, and ongoing services (He et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026), while multi-firm economies additionally study negotiation and market interaction (Sugiura et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Across these settings, earlier decisions shape the opportunities and constraints of subsequent action.

Planning and Commitment Coordination.

Maintaining a plan requires checking how actions and new observations affect the conditions for subsequent steps (Ghallab et al., 2016). Planning evaluations test plan generation, verification, and replanning (Valmeekam et al., 2023). Feedback-driven methods revise plans when observations depart from expectations (Sun et al., 2023), while coordination frameworks explicitly manage execution dependencies and detect stale joint plans (You et al., 2026). Coordination can also depend on agreements formed during earlier interactions. SCARCE studies how agents with separate objectives negotiate access to shared execution resources and develop agreements and norms that persist across tasks (Kumar et al., 2026). OutfitterBench examines a different coordination problem: whether a manager can keep customer commitments compatible with changing resource availability and subsequent allocations.

Intertemporal Resource Allocation.

A resource decision affects both current returns and what remains available for later work. Inventory control studies examine ordering under demand shifts and uncertain lead times (Baek et al., 2026). When agents also choose which work to accept, resource allocation and commitment formation become linked. In YC-Bench, accepted projects draw on a fixed workforce, with progress accumulating toward project deadlines; taking on additional work can overcommit shared employee effort (He et al., 2026). CEO-Bench links growth and investment to the capacity needed for continuing service (Chen et al., 2026), while EnterpriseArena examines how financing timing and scale affect future liquidity under delayed settlement and changing economic conditions (Han et al., 2026).

Reusable-resource allocation makes the duration of occupancy part of the economic decision: serving one customer temporarily removes capacity from other potential uses (Zhang and Cheung, 2022). Whereas project work can accumulate toward completion before a deadline, rental commitments require reusable capacity during specified future service intervals. OutfitterBench examines how agents keep such arrangements feasible while reassessing which resource uses to retain or revise.

3 OutfitterBench

OutfitterBench simulates an outdoor-equipment rental business. Rental provides a setting for reusable-resource allocation: accepting business commits capacity before later demand is known (Chen et al., 2017; Zhang and Cheung, 2022). To study feasibility maintenance and resource valuation together, we design the environment around three interacting features.

First, outdoor trips require complementary equipment to be ready together, while rental, return, and servicing change its availability. Agents must keep accepted bookings compatible with evolving supply and subsequent uses. Second, customers compete for shared rental capacity (Savin et al., 2005): reservations and uncertain walk-ins draw on the same fleet. Prices and capacity protection determine what commitments earn and which opportunities remain available. Third, agents can revise commitments and change fleet composition, but customer response delays, cancellation compensation, and resale losses make adjustments costly. Once the equipment-capital ceiling binds, new investment may require replacing existing assets.

We construct the product catalog from Taobao listings and use historical Beijing weather to model demand and operating conditions. Customer behavior and equipment operations follow explicit rules and probabilistic models. Figure 2 gives an overview of the environment.

3.1 Task, Interaction, and Objective

A season comprises 200 manager-decision days followed by 14 automatic settlement days, during which outstanding rentals, service work, and liabilities settle after new business ends. The objective is to maximize terminal business value: cash plus eligible equipment resale value, less outstanding liabilities. Rent generates income, while procurement, servicing, operating expenses, and customer compensation create costs. Section 4.3 defines the score and reported value gain.

Each morning, the environment processes deliveries, service work, returns, and eligible pickups. The agent receives an inbox and can query records, set prices, buy or sell equipment, arrange servicing, and handle bookings. At closing, the environment resolves outstanding pickup issues, serves walk-ins, charges daily costs, and advances the day. Each day starts a fresh model session. Business records persist, and the agent can maintain retrievable notes and a handoff for the next day.

Observations include finances, transactions, asset and contract states, service schedules, customer feedback, and the public calendar and weather forecast. Customer preferences are partly revealed through interactions; future requests and operating outcomes remain uncertain.

3.2 Customer Demand and Commitments

Reservations and walk-ins compete for the same fleet, linking current admissions to capacity available for later bookings. Both channels originate from a common pool of potential outings. For each intended outing day dd and trip type kk (overnight camping, picnic outings, or lightweight trips), the simulator samples the number of potential customer parties:

Nk,d∼Poisson⁡(λk,d).N_{k,d}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{k,d}). (1)

The rate λk,d\lambda_{k,d} varies with season and calendar. Weekends and public holidays concentrate demand; school holidays also increase weekday activity. Each party is assigned a channel and, for reservations, a booking lead time. Advance customers decide whether to submit a request using the forecast available that day for their trip; walk-ins respond to arrival-day weather. The agent sees the same public forecast.

For each outing, we sample party composition and rental duration by trip type and calendar, then generate required and optional equipment needs. Public service profiles translate these needs into suitable products and quantities using functional guarantees, such as temperature suitability, and per-item capacities, such as sleeping places. Budget and preference parameters come from predefined scenario distributions, allowing parties with similar needs to value equipment and rental convenience differently. Equipment choices within a reservation share budget and price-sensitivity parameters, with preferences also varying by category.

For advance inquiries, we use a random-utility model (Train, 2009) to compare complete rental plans with buying equipment, using gear already available to the party, or abandoning the trip. A product’s functional fit and quality contribute to both purchase and rental utility (Lancaster, 1966). Ownership benefits, service convenience, payments, and the rental deposit then affect the relative appeal of the alternatives. A quoted plan is acceptable when its utility exceeds that of the outside alternatives. These alternatives therefore constrain what customers are willing to pay for a rental plan. Walk-ins choose required equipment first; optional choices depend on those selections.

Advance requests specify equipment requirements, trip lengths, and permitted pickup dates. We include two forms to examine how agents choose which work to undertake and on what terms. Fixed-term offers provide customer-approved configurations and rents; the agent selects a plan and date or declines. For manager-priced inquiries, it proposes configurations and prices for customer approval. Equipment choices and prices shape both the return from a commitment and the capacity left for other opportunities, linking pricing with resource allocation (Bitran and Caldentey, 2003; Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004). Customer approval can directly confirm a quoted booking. Confirmation fixes products, quantities, dates, and prices as obligations that the agent must support or revise through later decisions.

Walk-ins are served automatically at closing using posted prices and ready equipment. The agent controls new walk-in occupancy through product- and date-specific limits on how many units those rentals can occupy. Walk-in rentals can extend into future booking windows, and new reservations can overlap earlier bookings. Through both channels, the agent commits capacity before knowing which later requests will arrive or what they will be worth.

To support learning from experience, the environment provides transaction histories, unfilled walk-in requests, and occasional noisy feedback on declined quotations, including concerns about price or equipment fit. Together with public product attributes, these records give agents evidence about how customer responses vary with equipment, prices, and trip conditions.

3.3 Shared Capacity and Resource Allocation

Meeting accepted commitments requires coordinating complementary assets whose readiness depends on prior rentals and shared turnaround capacity. The shop starts with 27 physical assets and can purchase from a 46-product catalog of tents, sleeping equipment, and picnic supplies. Different parties can draw on overlapping sets of suitable products, while their functional requirements limit substitution. A booking may require several equipment types together, so a shortage can prevent complete fulfillment even when other equipment is idle. Confirmed products remain binding unless the customer authorizes a change.

Each unit has its own condition, usage history, and operational status. Once rented, a unit becomes available again only after returning and completing required cleaning, repair, or maintenance. Returns enter a shared, capacity-limited cleaning queue and become available no earlier than the next day. Cleaning workload determines both the cleaning charge and the demand placed on the shared queue. The shared queue can delay readiness for other orders, even across equipment types or non-overlapping rental intervals.

Calendar and weather effects connect demand with these constraints. Holidays can bring more and longer trips while making renters more likely to extend their use; weather exposure changes cleaning workloads. Updated forecasts can prompt rescheduling or cancellation. Public information and operating history help anticipate these patterns, although individual outcomes remain uncertain.

The agent can accept bookings against expected deliveries, returns, and service completions, with units assigned at pickup. Confirmation records the agreed obligations without checking future capacity; the agent must arrange supply and keep later allocations compatible with existing bookings. Walk-in limits can protect bookings but also exclude rentals that would leave equipment ready again before the booked pickup. Figure 3 illustrates these competing uses.

As conditions change, the agent can reassess how and whether to support a commitment. Before pickup, it can propose revisions; customers respond the next day, and accepted terms take effect when the agent applies them. Substitutions or reduced delivery at pickup require authorization. Alternatively, the agent can cancel, refund unearned payments, and pay compensation that increases as pickup approaches. Waiting may improve information but leave fewer adjustment options. The agent compares the value of fulfillment with that of releasing capacity, accounting for agreed rent, further preparation, and the cost of changing course.

Fleet investments compete for a fixed equipment-capital allowance. Purchases require cash and must satisfy:

Bt+It≤Kmax,B_{t}+I_{t}\leq K_{\max}, (2)

where BtB_{t} is the historical acquisition cost still counted against the ceiling, and ItI_{t} is the cost of accepted inbound orders. Sale or disposal releases capital basis the next morning; until then, that basis remains in BtB_{t}. Revenue adds cash without raising KmaxK_{\max}. Owned equipment also incurs daily holding charges. Dealer resale value starts at 55% of purchase cost for intact, unused equipment and declines with condition and wear. When the ceiling binds, new purchases may require replacing existing assets. The agent compares the future uses of current and replacement assets, accounting for resale losses, holding costs, delivery waits, and existing booking obligations.

3.4 Data Sources and Parameterization

We use DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 as an auxiliary model to clean and structure product information from Taobao listings. Specifications provide functional attributes and per-item capacities; listing prices inform procurement costs and customers’ purchase alternatives, with selected adjustments recorded as benchmark settings. Products are matched to service profiles through rules on these attributes. The model also estimates product-level durability and cleaning workload from listed materials and construction details. Shared operating and cost rules translate these priors into wear accumulated through rental days and turnovers, cleaning-queue workloads, and service charges. Before freezing the data, we apply deterministic checks to verify profile membership against product specifications, validate capacities, and confirm a compatible profile for each rental product.

Customer budget and preference distributions, together with behavioral response parameters, are specified as benchmark settings.

Historical Beijing weather is replayed by month and day. We synthesize public forecasts by perturbing temperatures and weather categories using lead-time-dependent error settings. The demand and operating models use this shared weather sequence and the public calendar.

Random draws are indexed by event and world seed to support reproducible simulation. Appendices A and B provide operating rules and the evaluated configuration.

4 Evaluation Protocol

4.1 Models and Operating Protocol

We evaluate 7 model configurations on 2 world seeds, with one complete run per model–seed pair. We use GPT 6.1 Sol (Sol) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Opus) with high reasoning effort, and Kimi K3 (Kimi), GLM 5.2 (GLM), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0910 (DeepSeek), GPT 6 Luna (Luna), and MiMo V2.6 Flash (MiMo) with max reasoning effort.

Each run starts with 3,000 CNY, the same initial fleet, a 2,141.83 CNY equipment-capital ceiling, and a 15 CNY daily operating fee. Each evaluated season generates approximately 1,100 reservation requests. Agents receive the same business tools and instructions, fresh daily sessions, persistent records, and up to 200 model responses per day. Run and controller details appear in Appendix B.

Runs within each seed share the initial shop and seeded external processes; their decisions then produce different fleets, obligations, and customer interactions. The main results table, value paths in Figure 1, and main-text process diagnostics average seed-level measurements equally across these worlds. Appendix C reports individual outcomes for each model–seed pair.

4.2 Public-Information Rule Reference

We also run Calendar, a fixed operating policy, on both worlds. It uses a twelve-product assortment with fixed prices, replenishment targets, maintenance, and recovery rules. Using public asset states, return estimates, and service schedules, it accepts bookings with positive estimated direct contribution and sufficient projected calendar capacity.

Calendar allows one day for ordinary turnaround and interacts through agent-visible tools. It provides a reference for the value of consistent routines. Appendix B.4 gives its operating rules.

4.3 Operating Outcomes

At terminal day T=214T=214, the score of a solvent shop is

ST=CT+LT−ΛT,Δ​V=ST−V0,S_{T}=C_{T}+L_{T}-\Lambda_{T},\qquad\Delta V=S_{T}-V_{0}, (3)

where CTC_{T} is cash, LTL_{T} eligible equipment resale value, and ΛT\Lambda_{T} outstanding liabilities, including refundable deposits and unearned reservation payments. We report value creation Δ​V\Delta V relative to the initial business value V0=3,397.06V_{0}=3{,}397.06 CNY. Insolvency ends a run with a failure score. Model inference costs are recorded separately from business value; valuation details are in Appendix A.5.

Reservation deliveries and reliability describe the business served. Reliability is deliveries divided by deliveries plus merchant-caused failures; ordinary customer cancellations are excluded.

4.4 Process Diagnostics

We use four diagnostic families to relate operating outcomes to feasibility maintenance and resource valuation. All are computed from recorded states and actions without an LLM judge. Figure 4 reports equal-weight means across seeds, with ratios calculated within each run.

Pending-booking gaps.

After each day’s walk-ins, we check whether pending reservations have sufficient projected supply, using public asset states, service schedules, and return and delivery estimates. We report the share of observed booking–days with a shortage, both overall and one or two days before pickup. These rates track whether accepted bookings remain supported over time.

Action-induced new gaps.

We compare projected coverage immediately before and after a supported action, counting calls that leave a previously covered booking short. Rates are calculated separately for each action type over relevant successful calls. Quotation calls can directly confirm bookings after customer approval, so they can also create projected gaps for existing commitments. Walk-in rentals use customer-trip batches instead. This check identifies subsequent choices that undermine the supply supporting existing commitments.

Capital productivity.

We measure net service contribution per 100 capital-CNY-days. Contribution includes rent and damage deductions, less service costs and estimated equipment-use consumption; the denominator accumulates occupied equipment capital, including inbound purchases. This describes the return generated by the resources tied up over time, complementing the official score’s measure of total business value.

Unrealized gains from capacity relaxation.

At 40 fixed dates per run, we test whether slightly relaxing one product’s walk-in limit improves estimated contribution under a conservative supply check. The test holds stock, prices, commitments, and that day’s customer demand fixed. We report how often a positive estimated gain remains available under existing limits, and its mean across all sampled days, including zero-gain dates, using a three-day turnaround allowance. Candidates depend on each run’s fleet and existing limits, so the results describe remaining opportunities within that configuration. We therefore interpret these local estimates alongside the booking-gap rates.

Full definitions, individual results, and counts appear together in Appendix D, following the same four-family order. Trajectory analysis connects these measurements to recorded information, executed choices, and subsequent outcomes. Matched bookings and selected historical-state probes provide further comparisons, documented in Appendix E.

5 Results and Analysis

In this section, we compare agents’ long-term value creation and examine the resource-management patterns behind their performance. We focus on how agents maintain feasible plans and choose or revise resource allocations as opportunities change.

5.1 Overall Performance

All 14 LLM runs complete the season, and 10 create positive net value. Table 1 compares agents and the rule reference using equal-weight means over the two worlds. Individual results for each world are reported in Appendix C.1. The averaged paths in Figure 1 show the scale of the resulting differences; individual paths appear in Appendix C.3.

A fixed policy provides a substantial operating reference.

Calendar creates an average of about 1,120 CNY, outperforming Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and Opus on both seeds. Sol exceeds Calendar in each world, with mean value creation of +2,556.78 CNY. Luna and MiMo occupy the middle: they exceed Calendar in one world and fall below it in the other. Opus creates an average of +636.11 CNY, remaining profitable in both worlds without reaching the rule reference. These results distinguish profitable routine operation from the gains achievable through more effective management.

The scale of the operation does not determine this ordering. DeepSeek and Opus each deliver more bookings than Sol in both worlds. Calendar serves fewer reservations and earns 56–61% of its rental income from walk-ins. Its total rent is lower than Kimi’s, GLM’s, DeepSeek’s, and Opus’s in each world, but lower costs more than offset the difference. The decomposition in Appendix C.2 reconciles revenue, actual expenses, and recovered equipment value with the final score.

Schedule reliability alone does not explain the value differences. Sol, Opus, and Luna maintain relatively reliable schedules, but Sol creates substantially more value. We use the diagnostics in Figure 4 and recurring decisions in the trajectories to examine how agents maintain feasible resource plans and reassess the value of competing uses.

5.2 Intertemporal Feasibility Maintenance

Figure 4A shows mean projected gap rates of roughly 6–9% of pending booking–days for Sol, Opus, and Luna, compared with 21–34% for DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, and MiMo. These groups remain separated in each world. The trajectories reveal failures to apply operating rules consistently and reconcile new plans with existing obligations.

Applying operating rules consistently.

Because returned equipment must be cleaned before reuse, feasible schedules need turnaround room between consecutive rentals. Using each day’s closing equipment and booking ledger, we check whether newly confirmed bookings can be covered when units can be reused on their return day or instead require one day of turnaround. Requiring that extra day lowers coverage by 4.9–21.5 percentage points for DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, and MiMo, compared with 0–3.7 points for Sol, Opus, and Luna. More of the former group’s accepted schedules therefore depend on tightly spaced uses of the same equipment. Appendix D.6 gives the nominal-calendar assumptions and per-run results.

DeepSeek’s records show how an unstable working rule contributes to this pattern. Across its two runs, tables, pads, and chairs are repeatedly planned for their return date, despite separate correct applications of the cleaning requirement. Early corrections and cancellations do not make the rule govern later decisions consistently. In a late-season chair review, DeepSeek first recognizes that only one chair will be usable against three required. Seeing that the pickup is already confirmed for the chairs’ return day, it takes that existing confirmation as evidence that return-day reuse is allowed. Confirmation does not certify future supply, but DeepSeek records this interpretation and carries it into the next day. The chairs return on time but remain in cleaning at pickup. The failure follows a change to a working rule that DeepSeek had correctly applied in earlier decisions.

Coordinating new plans with existing commitments.

Across both runs, Sol repeatedly relates the quantities needed for upcoming bookings to the dates on which equipment is expected to become usable. These projections distinguish ready units from supply awaiting returns, cleaning, or delivery, and guide procurement, asset retention, and walk-in limits.

For a revised cookware schedule, Sol identifies a shortfall because a returning unit still needs cleaning before reuse. Cash is sufficient, but equipment capital is tied up. It sells a worn mat and buys another cookware unit after the capital allowance is released the next day. The order arrives two days later than estimated but before pickup. Before other asset sales, Sol checks remaining stock against near-term bookings. As returns and cleaning alter projected supply, it revises walk-in limits.

Maintaining coverage also requires checking whether new actions displace supply already promised elsewhere. Figure 4B shows that, on average, roughly 2–5% of relevant confirmation calls by Sol, Opus, and Luna introduce a new projected gap for a previously accepted booking, compared with 14–20% for DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, and MiMo. This separation holds in each world and recurs in the mean rates for quotation, fixed-offer acceptance, and walk-in exposure.

Sol nevertheless double-books its only long-runtime lantern. After querying an existing booking, it accepts another with overlapping rental dates and an earlier pickup, describing the offer as supportable. The new customer collects the lantern first; the booking accepted earlier is cancelled after renegotiation fails. Both obligations were visible when the new one was accepted, and the overlap does not depend on a return or cleaning forecast.

Opus correctly uses a cleaning-queue check to retain a table-and-chair pickup. On a later queue review, however, it prepares for a chair shortage several days away while overlooking sleeping bags and pads that will not be ready for the next morning’s booking. Both agents can organize supply for the task at hand. Their checks sometimes omit visible constraints relevant to other commitments. Appendix E.1 documents these preparation and joint-feasibility sequences.

5.3 Intertemporal Resource Valuation and Reallocation

Figure 4C reports mean capital productivity of CNY 1.38 per 100 capital-CNY-days for Sol, compared with 0.96–0.97 for Opus and Luna, with comparable capital occupancy. We examine how agents value commitments, carry feedback and prior evaluations into resource reallocation, and use available capacity while protecting future obligations.

Choosing which commitments to make and retain.

Accepting a commitment ties up future capacity for an agreed return and limits which later opportunities can be pursued. Opus completes more bookings than Sol in both worlds without attaining comparable business value. Among 77 pairs of fully delivered bookings matched by customer request, equipment, quantities, rental dates, and promised service, it charges less in 75; total agreed rent on these pairs is 30–37% lower than Sol’s. Its pricing records repeatedly recommend concessions after rejected quotes.

Those commitments also shape later admission decisions. Two four-day table, chair, and cookware bookings earn CNY 33 each for Opus and CNY 60 for Sol; Opus later sets aside other offers because the cookware is committed. Its larger completed operation is therefore accompanied by weaker value capture from the equipment-time it commits. Appendix E.2.1 gives the paired transactions and pricing records; Appendix C.2 provides the full-run accounting.

Once a concrete conflict brings competing obligations into view, however, even agents with weaker overall returns or unstable schedules can weigh exit costs against the value of retaining a booking. Facing two bookings that compete for a sleeping bag and pad, DeepSeek compares their rents, cancellation charges, and occupied time, then pays CNY 7.86 compensation before pickup to cancel the CNY 13.20 booking and preserve the CNY 73.50 booking, which is subsequently fulfilled. Similarly, when a tent conflict cannot be resolved by rescheduling, Opus compares buying another tent against early cancellation and exits the booking. The larger difference lies in how consistently such comparisons shape commitments and resource allocations throughout the season. Both decisions are documented under “Deliberate exit after economic comparison” in Appendix E.2.1.

Turning feedback and evaluations into resource reallocation.

When resources are fully committed, acting on new opportunities requires revisiting existing allocations and previously evaluated alternatives. Sol and Luna can both assess alternative investments, but differ in how those assessments shape later resource decisions. In one shared world, Luna already holds a higher-cost comfort-chair model (about CNY 103 per unit) when it evaluates a lower-cost comfort chair (about CNY 36) for expansion. It considers the candidate’s payback, delivery time, and an asset sale that could fund the purchase. About two weeks later, with nearly all capital committed, it reviews its higher-cost existing chair and supports retention through past rental income and continued earning potential. Luna mentions the lower-cost model as a product it does not currently own, without revisiting the earlier funding proposal. Luna continues buying and selling other equipment, but purchases the lower-cost comfort chairs more than two months after first assessing them.

Sol, by contrast, repeatedly carries demand comparisons into allocation decisions. After reviewing recent demand, fleet sizes, delivery time, and holding costs, it buys a sixth comfort chair rather than a seventeenth lightweight chair. The lightweight fleet has earned more total rent, but the additional comfort chair would enable six-person comfort-seating requests. Customer rejections of quoted lightweight-chair configurations prompt another adjustment: Sol checks that the remaining lightweight chairs cover near-term bookings, sells an unused chair, and buys another comfort chair once capital is released. As cold-weather demand weakens, Sol shifts from sleeping equipment to seating.

Sol more consistently carries investment assessments into later decisions about which assets to retain and replace. Between Luna’s initial assessment and eventual purchase, the shops receive walk-in requests for the same 141 comfort-chair units; Sol supplies 46 and Luna 16 under their respective fleets, prices, and capacity limits. Appendix E.2.2 documents the decision sequences and the scope of the walk-in and reservation comparisons.

Using available capacity while protecting commitments.

Future commitments require capacity at particular times, leaving intervening availability that may support additional work. In the MiMo and DeepSeek replays, many additional rentals would occupy equipment needed for upcoming bookings, leaving fewer opportunities that fit around the existing schedule. Figure 4D finds positive estimated contribution from a small limit relaxation without a new projected booking gap on an average of 31.25% of sampled days for Luna, compared with 12.50% for Sol. For Luna, they recur across products early and late in both seasons.

A sleeping-pad booking illustrates one way those opportunities are excluded. Luna blocks its ready three-person pad from walk-ins twelve days before pickup and keeps the restriction through the rental. In our capacity-relaxation test using the following day’s state, raising the limit by one unit admits an intervening rental scheduled to return a week before pickup, with rent exceeding its estimated cleaning and usage costs. The restriction protects a particular future use by closing a much longer available interval. The case highlights the value of matching protection to the timing and capacity required by a commitment. Unused opportunities also remain in both Sol runs. Appendix E.2.3 reports the rental intervals and local test results.

Effective preparation for individual commitments does not consistently extend to joint feasibility, while more reliable fulfillment can coexist with weak returns and delayed resource reallocation. Sol more effectively compares competing uses of equipment and capital, and carries these comparisons into supply preparation and fleet changes. Its scheduling conflicts and unused rental opportunities expose limits in both feasibility maintenance and value comparison, even in the strongest runs.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

We introduced OutfitterBench to study how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing the value of resource allocations as opportunities change. Calendar outperforms several LLM agents, while only the leading agent exceeds this fixed reference in both evaluated worlds. The trajectories reveal weaknesses both in sustaining feasible arrangements and in choosing worthwhile resource uses. Constraints correctly applied during preparation are sometimes omitted from later decisions. More reliable runs can still earn less from comparable bookings or delay capital reallocation.

Feasibility maintenance and resource valuation are coupled. Existing commitments restrict subsequent uses, while alternative returns and adjustment costs guide which arrangements are worth retaining or revising. Paying to exit a lower-value booking can preserve more valuable business, whereas replacing equipment can remove support for an existing obligation. Capacity-relaxation tests illustrate a further trade-off: more precise protection can admit intervening rentals with positive estimated contribution while preserving projected booking coverage. Long-horizon consistency thus requires stable use of operating constraints and selective revision of commitments and allocations.

These findings motivate testing decision support that combines dependable constraint checks with selective economic reassessment. Such support could link proposed changes to affected commitments and retain evaluated alternatives with the conditions that would make them worth revisiting. OutfitterBench provides a testbed for studying how agents maintain feasible plans while choosing and revising resource uses for long-term value.

7 Limitations

The environment draws on real product and weather records, but customer behavior is rule-based rather than LLM-driven, and costs and operating events follow simulation assumptions. Transfer to other markets or real operations remains untested. With only two world seeds and one run per model–seed pair, the stability of the observed rankings under broader sampling remains uncertain. Diagnostics and selected cases help interpret decisions without isolating each behavior’s contribution to the final score; capacity-relaxation tests do not follow subsequent agent decisions and thus do not estimate additional seasonal profit. We use fixed business tools and a daily-session controller, without a general-purpose shell such as Bash or coding-agent harnesses such as Codex or Claude Code.

Guide to the Appendices

Appendix A gives operating and scoring rules; Appendix B describes the evaluation protocol, agent instructions and tools, and Calendar. For the individual outcomes behind Table 1 and Figure 1, see Appendix C. Appendix D follows the four diagnostic families in Figure 4, with definitions and detailed results together. Appendix E documents the decision sequences discussed in Section 5.

Appendix A Operating Rules and Scoring

This appendix specifies the operating rules behind the decisions discussed in Sections 3 and 5. The evaluated parameter settings appear in Appendix B.1.

A.1 Asset Readiness and Servicing

Service Profiles specify functional guarantees and capacity per physical asset. The quotation workspace translates customer needs into quantities. Rental occupancy runs from pickup pp to scheduled morning return rr, over [p,r)[p,r), and may extend if the customer returns late.

Morning processing handles deliveries, service work, returns, and eligible pickups. Existing cleaning jobs receive capacity before newly returned equipment joins the queue. Cleaning processes 30 work points each morning at 0.50 CNY per point; workload varies with equipment and use. Repair and maintenance require cash and downtime while cumulative wear continues to constrain service life.

A.2 Booking Formation and Revision

Advance requests are manager-priced inquiries or fixed service offers, with one or two advertised dates. A quoted menu applies to both dates; the manager can select one authorized complete plan and one date. A single authorized plan with a single date confirms immediately. Other unresolved confirmations default at closing to the original date and customer-preferred plan. Fixed offers are accepted as whole plans.

Each line selects one product/Profile pair, with asset quantity equal to the ceiling of service units divided by capacity per asset. Confirmation locks products, quantities, dates, prices, and deposits; physical assets are assigned at pickup. A 25% prepayment is held as unearned revenue until pickup. All selected lines, including optional items, become obligations. Resource coverage is checked by the manager. Additional rental days are discounted relative to the first day.

Protecting and revising bookings.

Walk-in limits cap new occupancy by SKU and date. Existing rentals continue, and the manager must allow for return and cleaning when setting these limits. Proactive renegotiation proposes concrete changes at least two days before pickup; the permitted inquiry returns the next day, and an accepted change requires explicit application that day. Pickup-time recovery separately obtains current customer authorization for substitutions or reduced delivery, with delivery checked at closing. The manager evaluates how either change affects other bookings.

A.3 Equipment Capital, Exit, and Trials

Let K0K_{0} be the initial fleet’s historical basis and HH additional headroom. The fixed ceiling is Kmax=K0+H=2,141.83K_{\max}=K_{0}+H=2{,}141.83. With BtB_{t} owned basis still charged and ItI_{t} accepted inbound basis, available capital is

Ktfree=Kmax−Bt−It.K_{t}^{\mathrm{free}}=K_{\max}-B_{t}-I_{t}. (4)

Purchases also require cash and warehouse space. Delivery transfers basis from ItI_{t} to BtB_{t}. Sale proceeds arrive immediately, while sale or disposal releases historical basis the following day; pending releases remain in BtB_{t} until then. The ceiling remains fixed as the business earns revenue. The warehouse limit is 5,000 units, making capital the tighter fleet-expansion constraint.

Owned equipment incurs a daily capital holding charge of 0.12​Pa/3650.12P_{a}/365, where PaP_{a} is its acquisition basis, plus on-site non-rented storage charges.

Supplier trials.

Temporary supplier trials provide another source of equipment: at most four accepted trials per season and one active at a time, with handling and usage fees, a fixed return window, and a three-rental limit. Returning a trial item removes it from service.

A.4 Compensation and Refunds

Each promised line receives a first-day guarantee basis GiG_{i} at confirmation: first-day unit tariff times quantity for ordinary quotes, or the whole-line first-day amount for fixed offers. For affected original obligations AA and NN days’ notice,

α⁡(N)\displaystyle\alpha(N) =1−0.75​min⁡(max⁡(N,0)7,1),\displaystyle=1-0.75\min\!\left(\frac{\max(N,0)}{7},1\right), (5)
CA​(N)\displaystyle C_{A}(N) =rnd0.01⁡(α⁡(N)​∑i∈AGi).\displaystyle=\operatorname{rnd}_{0.01}\!\left(\alpha(N)\sum_{i\in A}G_{i}\right). (6)

At least seven days’ notice costs 25% of the basis; same-day nonfulfillment costs 100%. Whole-order failure covers all original lines, while agreed reduced delivery covers the missing lines. Unprovided rent is refunded or credited separately, discharging the corresponding payment liability.

The original basis persists through revisions, and settled obligations are charged once. Ordinary customer cancellation has no merchant compensation. A manager can cancel before pickup without waiting for a risk alert. The evaluated configuration uses contract-level settlement without an additional global reputation penalty.

A.5 Terminal Valuation and Runoff

Owned asset aa has nominal dealer value

Va=0.55​Pa​ca​max⁡(0,1−wa)0.65,V_{a}=0.55P_{a}c_{a}\max(0,1-w_{a})^{0.65}, (7)

subject to monetary rounding, where cac_{a} is condition and waw_{a} cumulative wear. An intact unused asset has a 55% recovery baseline.

Eligible terminal assets are available, damaged, cleaning, repairing, or under maintenance. Paid repairs use post-repair condition. Unpaid cleaning is deducted once from the dealer pool, floored at zero. Rented, supplier-owned, retired, sold, and unreceived equipment has zero terminal owned value.

The within-season curves use contract-adjusted value: cash plus equipment value, less deposit, unearned-revenue, and credit liabilities. This includes active owned rentals at expected recoverable value, net of expected cleaning and including expected damage deductions. Prepaid equipment still in transit is valued at 55% of its purchase cost. Other owned equipment uses dealer value less unpaid cleaning. Future reservation rents are not counted as profit before service. Once contracts and orders are settled, the curves’ terminal endpoints reconcile with the official score.

The fourteen settlement days process existing returns and services, with no further manager decisions or new pickups. The daily operating fee stops; holding and outstanding service costs continue. Refund or compensation shortfalls can draw up to 300 CNY of protective credit with a 25% fee. Required-payment insolvency ends the run with the negative recorded cash shortfall.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocol and Rule Reference

B.1 Shared Study Settings

All 14 model runs share the environment code, catalog, business instructions, and tool schema. The initial fleet is fixed across seeds. Table 2 lists the common economic settings. Result tables group runs by seed and use the same model order as Table 1, with Calendar last. The warehouse limit is set to 5,000 weighted units, leaving it slack rather than making storage the principal constraint.

The decision calendar spans April 1–October 17, 2026, followed by automatic settlement through October 31. Historical Beijing weather is replayed by month and day. Potential customers are assigned to the reservation channel with probability 0.7, with booking leads of 1–14 days. Realized channel shares also depend on customer decisions and service availability.

Weather data in the public release.

The reported experiments use frozen Visual Crossing weather data. The public release replaces this input with an openly licensed Beijing series constructed from NOAA observations and ERA5/ERA5-Land reanalysis, retaining the same business rules and scoring.

B.2 Controller, Memory, and Execution

All runs configure temperature 1.0, an 800,000-character within-day context budget, 200 responses per day, and 40,000 responses per season. A response can batch up to five independent read-only queries; state-changing calls execute individually. Errors and responses without tools consume rounds. Budget reminders state the remaining rounds, and unfinished days close automatically at the daily limit.

Business state persists across fresh daily sessions. Named notes can be searched, read, replaced, or deleted, with a 40,000-character body limit per document. The agent retrieves notes explicitly; the closing handoff is supplied automatically the next day. The complete system prompt and tool inventory appear in Appendix B.5.

Table 3 reports model and tool calls alongside token use. Model inference costs are separate from the shop’s score.

B.3 Aggregation and Inclusion

Each model has one complete run on each of the two seeds. For a run-level measure qq, the reported model mean is

q¯m=qm,42+qm,732.\bar{q}_{m}=\frac{q_{m,42}+q_{m,73}}{2}. (8)

Rates are computed within each run before averaging. A complete diagnostic mean requires defined values on both seeds; a missing or inapplicable observation is not replaced with zero. Counts in the detailed tables retain their own denominators.

Figure 1 applies the same averaging at every completed day to contract-adjusted value minus initial official value. Its final point equals mean official value creation. All full-season comparisons use complete, matching-version trajectories. Adding a model leaves the world generator, metric definitions, and existing model results unchanged.

B.4 Public-Information Rule Reference

We designed Calendar around a fixed assortment and pricing policy, with daily checks on booking capacity. Its twelve products cover core camping and picnic needs, with stock targets of two to ten units per product and first-day tariffs of 3.75–10 CNY per item. These hand-specified settings remain fixed across days and seeds. Replenishment follows a fixed priority within cash and capital limits, retaining a 500 CNY reserve net of customer liabilities. It stops in the last thirty decision days.

The calendar uses current assets, public returns, service-job dates, inbound estimates, and commitments. A booking is accepted when estimated rent less ordinary cleaning is positive and it introduces no projected resource conflict.

Calendar allows one day of ordinary turnaround, evaluates advertised dates separately, and follows current customer authorization for recovery. It does not initiate supplier trials or proactive renegotiation. The calendar is rebuilt daily from public tools under the same 200-round interaction limit. The policy’s internal computation is not token-metered.

Both rule runs finish without insolvency, tool errors, or budget exhaustion; the maximum daily interaction count is 73. Their environment, data, and business instructions match the model runs. Their outcomes and channel revenues appear alongside the models in Appendix C. Extended replay diagnostics cover the LLM runs.

B.5 Agent Instructions and Tools

B.5.1 System Prompt and Daily Inputs

All evaluated LLM runs use the same system prompt and the same 43 tools. The prompt below is reproduced verbatim from the saved run artifacts; only its line wrapping is changed for presentation.

Each day also supplies a morning observation and, when available, the previous day’s handoff. Within a day, the agent receives tool results and remaining-budget notices. Named notes are retrieved through the memory tools. Detailed public operating rules are available on demand through read_business_rules, under six topics: assets, finance, procurement, reservations, scoring, and workspace. Thus, the fixed prompt establishes the task and interaction rules, while tool queries provide detailed rules and the current business state.

You manage a seasonal outdoor-equipment rental shop in Beijing. All money is CNY. Keep the shop solvent and maximize its official final value. Use business tools to perform actions; ordinary text and notes do not alter contracts or complete business operations. Detailed public rules are available through read_business_rules; omit topics for its directory or request relevant topics.

Manager decisions, new demand and pickups end on Day 200. Automatic runoff continues through Day 214, when final value is scored; there are no manager actions during runoff. For a solvent shop, final value = cash + final owned-equipment net dealer value - refundable deposits - unearned reservation revenue - refund-protection credit liabilities. An unpaid required payment ends the run in insolvency after any applicable refund protection. See scoring rules for terminal eligibility, deductions and insolvency scoring. Model usage is recorded separately and does not reduce shop cash or the official score.

A newly delivered, unused, intact owned asset has a 55% nominal recovery baseline relative to its recorded acquisition cost. Actual value depends on condition and wear; the full formula and settlement rules are in the scoring handbook. Deposits and unearned prepayments are liabilities, not profit. Cash, durable-capital headroom and warehouse space are separate constraints; capital headroom is not additional cash.

Each day opens after automatic morning processing, including deliveries, returns, service jobs and eligible reservation pickups. Closing resolves pending reservation defaults and pickup risks before walk-ins, charges daily costs and advances the day. Contractual return dates and supplier delivery estimates are not guarantees of physical availability. Customers can continue using rented equipment without approval. Normal returned equipment must pass through cleaning and cannot be rented again on its return day. Current asset status and service terms determine whether it can be used now.

A quotation may create a binding commitment immediately or at close. Customer authorization and successful confirmation do not certify inventory or scheduling feasibility. Every committed line, including a selected optional line, is binding; changes require the applicable customer-authorization process. Merchant cancellation or nonfulfillment incurs refunds/credits and compensation under the disclosed rules. Initial authorization, later modification and actual pickup are different events; current contract terms and settlement receipts record what has occurred. Walk-ins use posted prices, while reservations use their own locked terms. Offers without a posted price do not serve walk-ins. Pricing units and each operation’s permissions, deadlines and default consequences are described by its tools and the handbook.

Every business day starts a fresh model session. Business state and named memory documents persist; previous days’ reasoning, ordinary assistant text and transcripts are not supplied. Retrieve saved notes through memory tools; they are not automatically loaded. A closing handoff is supplied only on the next day. Older same-day messages may leave the context window.

There are at most 200 model responses per day. Each response consumes a round, including responses without tools or with errors. Budget notices state the remaining rounds, including the next response. At the daily limit, permitted tools from the last response execute before automatic close if the day remains open. You may batch at most 5 independent read-only tools in one response. State changes, memory writes/deletions and close_business_day must each be the only tool request in a response. Invalid batches execute nothing. Tool descriptions identify read-only and state-changing operations. Call close_business_day when today’s decisions are complete.

B.5.2 Available Tools

Table 4 lists the complete tool inventory. Tool names and read/write classifications follow the evaluated interface; the descriptions summarize their purpose. Read-only queries may be batched as specified in the prompt. State-changing calls, note updates, and day closing are submitted individually. Tool descriptions and the public handbook provide parameter requirements, authorization conditions, deadlines, and default outcomes.
