Appendix D Diagnostic Methods and Detailed Results

The four families follow Figure 4A–D, with definitions and results together. Results are grouped by seed. These diagnostics cover the LLM runs; Calendar’s operating results appear in Appendix C.

D.1 Observation Windows and Readiness Projection

Tables cover the complete season and retain numerators and denominators. Model means average two run-level measurements (Appendix B.3).

The pending-booking and action-induced-gap diagnostics project supply from public asset states and schedules. Ready units are available today. FIFO cleaning completes after cumulative remaining work divided by daily capacity, rounded up to at least one more morning. Repair and maintenance use their scheduled ready dates.

Rented equipment uses the latest public estimated return, or its approved or promised return, plus the turnaround allowance gg. Overdue assets without a future return estimate remain outside projected supply. Inbound owned orders use a public ETA later than today. Trial supply ends at its deadline and is excluded once return is pending or no rental starts remain. The booking calendar includes confirmed and at-risk commitments, staged products, and authorized omissions.

A booking occupies product capacity over [p,r+g)[p,r+g), with pickup pp and scheduled return rr. The standard allowance is g=1g=1. Checks at day tt compare product quantities on dates from tt onward. A booking has a gap if total demand exceeds projected supply in any product–date cell it occupies. All bookings using that cell are marked, rather than allocating the shortfall by priority. Future cleaning congestion, damage, late returns, and service-life exhaustion can change actual availability; later information can also restore supply excluded by an earlier projection.

D.2 Pending-Booking Gaps

After each day’s walk-ins, the evaluator checks pending bookings with future pickup dates. For observed booking–days ℋ\mathcal{H}, the rate is

100​∑(c,t)∈ℋ𝟏​[c has a projected gap at t]|ℋ|.100\frac{\sum_{(c,t)\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbf{1}[\text{$c$ has a projected gap at $t$}]}{|\mathcal{H}|}. (9)

Each booking retains its identity across revisions and may contribute on multiple days. A gap can end through improved projected supply, pickup, or cancellation. The measure therefore describes support for retained commitments, alongside the delivery outcomes in Appendix C.1.

Table 7 gives the overall and near-pickup results behind Figure 4A. Near-pickup observations have one or two days until pickup; this is not a fixed cohort followed through recovery.

D.3 Action-Induced New Gaps

For each supported successful action, replay compares projected coverage immediately before and after execution. An action is relevant when it changes a product used by a pre-existing pending booking. It introduces a new gap when a booking present on both sides changes from covered to short. The rate counts gap-introducing calls over relevant calls, separately for each action type. One call counts once even if several bookings become short; removing a booking is not counted as creating a gap for that booking.

Walk-in rentals are checked separately. Actual rentals are grouped by customer trip and added sequentially to the pre-walk-in calendar. A batch counts when it introduces a shortage for a previously covered booking. Its denominator is all actual walk-in rental batches, rather than manager tool calls. The same one-day turnaround allowance is used.

Table 8 gathers the four series in Figure 4B, keeping their different exposure denominators separate.

D.4 Capital Productivity

Let Πcash\Pi^{\mathrm{cash}} be rental revenue and damage deductions less cleaning, repair, maintenance, holding, reservation compensation, and supplier-trial fees over the season. This service contribution excludes fixed daily operating fees and equipment purchase/sale cash flows.

For an owned asset aa, a rental of dd scheduled days has estimated linear use consumption

ua​(d)=Pa​(dLad+1Lac),u_{a}(d)=P_{a}\left(\frac{d}{L_{a}^{d}}+\frac{1}{L_{a}^{c}}\right), (10)

where PaP_{a} is acquisition cost and Lad,LacL_{a}^{d},L_{a}^{c} are the public day and cycle limits. The cycle term is omitted when absent. Each additional possession day adds Pa/LadP_{a}/L_{a}^{d}. Recorded daily consumption is used where available and otherwise reconstructed with the same rounding. Denote the seasonal total by UuseU^{\mathrm{use}}.

Using the capital quantities in Appendix A.3,

Qcap=100​Πcash−Uuse∑t=1T(Bt+It).Q^{\mathrm{cap}}=100\frac{\Pi^{\mathrm{cash}}-U^{\mathrm{use}}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(B_{t}+I_{t})}. (11)

The denominator accumulates day-end occupied capital, including inbound orders and basis awaiting release. The unit is CNY per 100 capital-CNY-days. Trial equipment contributes service income and fees without owned basis or an owned-wear charge.

Table 9 provides the components and the individual values behind Figure 4C. This measure describes returns per occupied capital-time; Appendix C.2 separately reconciles total business value using actual costs and dealer values.

D.5 Unrealized Gains from Capacity Relaxation

The test asks whether a small relaxation of a walk-in limit improves estimated service contribution under a conservative supply check. It samples days 5,10,…,2005,10,\ldots,200: forty dates fixed independently of model results.

A candidate raises one product’s existing finite occupancy limits by one over configured dates in [t,t+14][t,t+14], clipped to the season. In a copy of the pre-walk-in state, the evaluator applies the capacity tool and reruns that day’s walk-ins with the same stock, prices, commitments, and customers. Only products with finite limits contribute candidates; the set therefore depends on the agent’s fleet and prior decisions.

Let Jt​(a)J_{t}(a) be rent agreed in the resulting rentals less normal cleaning and owned-use consumption or trial fees. The estimate uses information at the branch, excluding future damage and late-return outcomes. The unchanged branch must reproduce the observed transactions.

Safety allowances g∈{1,3,7}g\in\{1,3,7\} are tested separately. Walk-ins and bookings occupy [p,r+g)[p,r+g), reserving gg turnaround days starting on the scheduled return day rr. Wherever a candidate increases occupancy, walk-in use and existing booking demand must fit the quantity available at branch start. This test reserves capacity without anticipating new returns or purchases.

For candidates 𝒜tg\mathcal{A}_{t}^{g} that pass, estimated improvement is

Δtg=max⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{g}=\max\bigl( {0}∪\displaystyle\{0\}\cup (12)
OPEN{Jt​(a)−Jt​(0):a∈𝒜tg}).\displaystyle\{J_{t}(a)-J_{t}(0):a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{g}\}\bigr).

The mean includes all forty sampled dates, including those with no improving candidate. An improving date has a gain of at least 0.01 CNY and counts once even when several products qualify.

Table 10 reports the g=3g=3 results used in Figure 4D alongside the g=1,7g=1,7 checks. A larger value indicates more estimated gains left in the recorded configuration; a smaller value alone does not establish better allocation. Each branch changes one product’s limits over the specified date range but reruns only the sampled day’s walk-ins. Subsequent policy decisions are not rerun, so these estimates cannot be added into recoverable season profit. Appendix E.2.3 shows the rental intervals behind representative positive tests.

D.6 Sensitivity to Turnaround in the Nominal Calendar

This supplementary check asks how tightly new bookings are spaced under different turnaround assumptions. It uses the closing book on the day of confirmation, rather than the public-readiness projection above. Supply consists of initial owned units and accepted purchases, less exits. Owned orders count from acceptance; delivered trial units count until return or their deadline. Physical delivery, cleaning congestion, walk-ins, damage, and later service-life exhaustion are abstracted out.

A new booking is covered when quantity fits at every product–date cell it uses. Table 11 reports coverage for g=0,1,2g=0,1,2, where g=0g=0 permits return-day reuse. The change from g=0g=0 to g=1g=1 supports the comparison in Section 5.2. Bookings terminated on the confirmation day are excluded. Procurement and revisions completed that day affect the result.

D.7 Feasibility and Resource Returns Within Each World

Figure 8 relates pending-booking gaps to capital productivity within each seed. It complements the mean profile in Figure 4: comparatively reliable schedules can still produce different returns from occupied capital. The panels retain world-specific variation using identical axes.

D.8 Replay Integrity

Replay uses the recorded environment version and runtime data and checks executed actions against their recorded receipts. Unchanged local branches must reproduce the relevant transactions and balances before alternatives are evaluated. A mismatch or incomplete branch stops the calculation. The detailed tables are generated from these completed reports; the presentation layer does not run new agent decisions.

Appendix E Evidence for the Trajectory Analysis

The subsections follow the two themes and five topics in Sections 5.2–5.3. Notes, handoffs, and visible responses record the agent’s assessment; receipts and asset histories establish actions and outcomes. Dates are simulation days and amounts are CNY. Local tests follow Appendix D.

E.1 Intertemporal Feasibility Maintenance

E.1.1 Applying Operating Rules Consistently

In seed 42, DeepSeek had recorded and applied the cleaning rule by day 39, including cancelling bookings 054 and 064. On days 144–145, however, it again planned to use sleeping pads on their return day for bookings 290 and 296. Two sleeping pads returned on time but became ready the following day; the cancellations cost 14.80 in total.

The later chair review makes the change in its working rule explicit. Booking 383 was already confirmed on day 177. On day 178, DeepSeek first counts one ready chair against three required. Seeing the pickup confirmed for the returning chairs’ return date, it then treats confirmation as evidence that same-day reuse is permitted. It records the new interpretation and carries it into the day-179 note. The chairs return normally on day 180 but finish cleaning on 181, missing the pickup. Cancellation costs 16, with a separate refund of the 4 prepayment. This sequence concerns reassessment of an existing booking: the agent had previously applied the rule correctly, then changed it while interpreting its own commitment.

A separate occurrence appears in seed 73. DeepSeek revises a four-table estimate for day 19 to two after recognizing that the returning tables remain unavailable, followed by cancellation of bookings 010 and 024. Together, the records show recurrence across both runs.

E.1.2 Coordinating New Plans with Existing Commitments

Preparing supply across financial and physical delays.

In Sol seed 73, a revised cookware schedule leaves a returning unit unavailable for another pickup until cleaning is complete. The shop needs a fourth unit. Cash is sufficient, but equipment capital is committed. Sol sells a worn mat on day 23, buys the 27.90 cookware unit after capital is released on 24, and receives it on 30 rather than the estimated 28. The new unit supplies booking 026 on day 33. The sequence connects a future shortage to an asset exit, next-day funding, procurement, and a delivery that still arrives before the obligation.

Sale–release–purchase sequences recur in Sol seed 42 on days 40–41, 52–53, 60–61, and 128–129. The capital choices in Appendix E.2.2 provide additional seed-73 sequences. This execution pattern also occurs in Kimi seed 42: after a rejected date proposal, it sells a chair on day 152 for 14.30 and buys a 32.61 mat after capital release on 153. Arrival on 158 supplies two day-165 bookings with rents of 39 and 13 and no compensation.

Applying the same source of readiness information.

Opus seed 42 receives a day-128 counteroffer on day 124 for booking 149. A cleaning-queue check shows that the table and chairs will be ready for the original day-125 pickup, which it retains and fulfills. On day 129, another queue query shows the sleeping bags and pads for booking 193 ready on day 131, after its day-130 pickup. Opus continues preparing for a chair shortage on day 133 without changing booking 193’s supply plan. The booking is cancelled on 130, with 10 compensation and a separate 2.50 prepayment refund. Both reviews obtain relevant queue information; they differ in which obligations that information governs.

Accepting an overlapping commitment.

In Sol seed 42, booking 093 is accepted on day 78 for days 90–92 and booking 097 on day 82 for days 89–92. Both require the shop’s sole long-runtime lantern. Before accepting 097, Sol queries the prior booking. Its visible responses then describe the new offer as coverable and supportable. It recognizes the double booking on day 88. The overlap exists during rental, independently of cleaning assumptions.

A local check reproduces the preceding actions: accepting 097 introduces a shortage for both bookings, while declining it leaves 093 covered on that product. Renegotiation for 093 fails; 097 takes the lantern on day 89, and 093 is cancelled on 90 with 40.50 compensation. The pre-acceptance record indicates a feasibility misjudgment rather than a deliberate economic choice to exit the earlier obligation.

Maintaining protection after acceptance.

Sol seed 42 accepts booking 086 on day 72 for a tent on days 83–86. That tent is rented to a walk-in on day 81, returns normally on 84, and finishes cleaning on 85. Booking 086 is cancelled on 83 with 12.53 compensation. The walk-in also earns revenue; the sequence identifies an unprotected obligation rather than a net-profit estimate for refusing that customer.

Other records show protection being updated with supply. In seed 73, Sol follows day-23 and day-24 acceptances with future occupancy limits, while reopening a one-day window for a chair and mat. On day 183, after customers refuse date changes, it counts six ready comfort chairs and four finishing cleaning before seven are required the next morning. It opens two chairs to current one-day walk-ins and sets the next day’s limit to zero. All five day-184 bookings are delivered. No extra chair rental occurs on 183, so this episode documents executed capacity adjustment rather than realized additional income.

E.2 Intertemporal Resource Valuation and Reallocation

E.2.1 Choosing Which Commitments to Make and Retain

Matched service and different agreed rents.

The Opus–Sol comparison matches world seed, customer request, rental dates, exact products, quantities, and promised service profiles. Both bookings must be completed with no omitted promised item or compensation, and with contracted products delivered unchanged. Optional items excluded before commitment are outside the service signature. The sample covers manager-quoted inquiries; initial agreed dates must also coincide. Table 12 reports the matched transactions.

Two seed-42 bookings each rent a table, two comfort chairs, and cookware for four days. Opus charges 33 and Sol 60. Opus’s later notes cite cookware committed to these bookings when setting aside other fixed-price offers. Its pricing records repeatedly recommend concessions after rejection, although higher-price attempts also occur. The match holds delivered service terms constant; the two shops still have different business histories. Channel revenues and costs are reported separately in Appendix C.2.

A complementary Sol seed-73 decision illustrates choosing lower rent for resource compatibility. On day 78, the customer authorizes three plans for days 87–90: 39 for a table, lightweight chairs, and cookware; 43 with comfort chairs instead; and 41 with comfort chairs and a frying pan. Sol selects the 39 plan as booking 089 rather than the customer’s preferred 43 plan. Its note preserves comfort-chair and pan capacity for booking 086 and a possible late return of 087. All three bookings complete without compensation. The record shows the choice and its stated resource rationale; it does not assign a measured value to the retained flexibility.

Deliberate exit after economic comparison.

On day 184, DeepSeek seed 42 compares bookings 373 and 387, both due on 185. Together they exceed usable supply by one cold-weather sleeping bag and one foam pad; cancelling either removes both shortages. Their rents are 73.50 and 13.20. DeepSeek compares rent, cancellation costs, occupied time, and the higher compensation and allocation risk of waiting until pickup. It chooses to retain 373 and cancel 387 a day early.

The executed cancellation pays 7.86 compensation and refunds the 3.30 prepayment. Booking 373 completes for 73.50 net rent and no compensation. As specified in Appendix A.4, the prepayment refund settles an existing liability; compensation is the additional exit cost.

Opus seed 73 makes an investment-versus-exit comparison on day 183. Booking 331 promises a tent and other equipment on days 189–192 for 29, but its tent overlaps another booking and a date change has been refused. A second tent costs 89.61, has an estimated two-day delivery, and fits the recorded 108.26 capital headroom. Those estimates leave time and capital for procurement six days before pickup.

Opus weighs the acquisition–resale difference, the booking’s rent, possible remaining-season walk-in use, and a 5.18 early-exit charge. It judges the added investment unattractive and notes that cancellation also releases the other equipment. The receipt confirms cancellation, 5.18 compensation, and a 7.25 prepayment refund. Its valuation is approximate, and it remains uncertain about authorization for a cheaper tent substitute. The example records an explicit comparison of further investment with exit.

E.2.2 Turning Feedback and Evaluations into Resource Reallocation

Sol: comparing and implementing alternative investments.

In seed 73, Sol sells a worn lantern on day 41 for 2.40, releasing its 30.90 capital basis the next morning. It compares a sixth comfort chair at 35.90, a replacement lantern at 30.90, and a three-person pad at 40. Its review considers recent demand, fleet sizes, delivery times, and remaining holding costs. Five comfort chairs have supplied 16 units over 37 asset-days for 119.25 rent in the previous thirty days; sixteen lightweight chairs have supplied 69 units over 112 asset-days for 278.96.

Sol buys the comfort chair on day 42. It rejects adding a seventeenth lightweight chair despite that fleet’s larger total rent: the sixth comfort chair would enable six-person comfort requests. It judges two remaining lanterns sufficient and the pad’s delivery too late for the nearest need. On day 45, further rejections of lightweight-chair configurations and limited comfort supply prompt another adjustment. Sol sells an unused lightweight chair for 14.30, after checking that fifteen retained units cover twelve required by upcoming bookings alongside its walk-in allowance. It buys another comfort chair on 46 after capital is released.

Later, on days 127–128, sparse demand for cold-weather bags and upcoming bookings using warm-weather bags support selling one cold-weather bag while retaining two. Repeated group-demand limits and a nine-chair concurrent requirement support the seating purchases. Sol waits for the sold bag’s 99 capital basis to be released before completing them. These sequences connect demand comparisons, retained obligations, and executed changes.

Luna: an earlier assessment in a later holding decision.

In seed 73, Luna evaluates a cheaper comfort chair on day 49. It considers two units at 35.90 each instead of the existing 102.60 model, discussing group demand, payback, delivery, and sale of a table with 82 capital basis to fund the investment. This is a proposed purchase, with procurement uncertainty also noted.

On day 65, with only 0.98 capital headroom, Luna reviews the higher-cost chair and supports retention through 37.75 of rental income already earned, low ongoing costs, and further earning potential. It mentions the cheaper model as a product it does not currently own, without returning to the earlier funding proposal. The purchase of four cheaper chairs occurs on day 116, after sales on 115. Luna continues other equipment transactions in the interval, including a mat replacement on days 85–86; the delay concerns this particular investment rather than all fleet management.

Demand served and reservation business mix.

Over days 49–115, both shops receive 43 walk-in comfort-chair requests for 141 units. Sol supplies 46 units across 16 served requests and Luna 16 across 7. These are rental occurrences, not distinct assets. They describe business served under the shops’ respective fleets, prices, and limits.

For full-season context on seed 73, the common manager-quoted requests yield 149 completed bookings for Sol and 148 for Luna, with net collected rent of 4,181.67 and 3,163.91 and committed asset-days of 967 and 845. Chair service accounts for 410 and 298 asset-days: Sol’s split is 148 lightweight plus 262 comfort, compared with Luna’s 256 plus 42. These reservation totals cover the full season and both chair classes, whereas the 141-unit comparison concerns comfort-chair walk-ins during the investment interval.

E.2.3 Using Available Capacity While Protecting Commitments

A protected interval longer than the booking requires.

Luna seed 73 has a ready three-person pad on day 134 but blocks it from walk-ins through day 149 for booking 161, whose pickup is on 146. A local test on day 135 admits an intervening rental scheduled to return on 139, one week before that pickup. Rent exceeds estimated normal cleaning and usage costs by 9.76. The candidate passes the one-, three-, and seven-day turnaround checks in Appendix D.5.

The best qualifying daily candidates span nine products in each Luna run, in both early and late periods. Table 10 gives all models’ frequencies and estimated gains, including dates with no improvement.

Remaining opportunities in Sol’s configurations.

For Sol’s cookware, the day-80 test in seed 42 adds a rental scheduled to return on 81, earning 4.00−1.25−0.186=2.5644.00-1.25-0.186=2.564 after cleaning and estimated use. The day-135 test in seed 73 adds one due on 136, earning 3.50−1.25−0.186=2.0643.50-1.25-0.186=2.064. Both pass all three checks.
